existing.description_short: SEC Drops 60%+ of Crypto Enforcement Cases in Mass Regulatory Capitulation
existing.description_long: Within weeks of Trump's inauguration, the Securities and Exchange Commission under acting chair Mark Uyeda began systematically dropping enforcement actions against the crypto industry, which had spent more than $100 million supporting Trump's election. By February 21, 2025, the SEC dismissed its nearly two-year case against Coinbase, the largest U.S. crypto exchange, which had been charged with operating as an unregistered securities exchange. On March 20, 2025, the SEC dropped its four-year case against Ripple Labs and its XRP token. The agency also dropped or froze cases against Kraken, Gemini, Binance, and Robinhood. A December 2025 New York Times investigation found that the SEC had eased up on more than 60% of the crypto cases that were in progress at the start of Trump's second term — a retreat from a single industry with no legal precedent. The investigation into Justin Sun, who had invested $45 million in Trump's World Liberty Financial, was settled in March 2025 for $10 million with no admission of wrongdoing, after being paused following his WLF investment. Senator Elizabeth Warren demanded explanations for the apparent connection between Sun's investment in the Trump family business and the SEC's decision to drop its case against him. The mass regulatory pullback directly enriched the crypto industry that had funded Trump's election while benefiting the Trump family, which held billions in crypto assets subject to SEC oversight.

description_long: Public Service Loan Forgiveness offers federal student-loan forgiveness to eligible borrowers after ten years of qualifying payments while working in qualifying public-service jobs. Teachers, nurses, firefighters, social workers, and other public employees may rely on the program when weighing public-service salaries against other work. The supplied account says the Trump administration issued new interpretations in February 2025 that disqualified some categories of workers and froze hundreds of thousands of pending applications. Borrowers who had chosen lower-paying jobs in anticipation of forgiveness described the changes as a broken promise. Such changes could affect recruitment and retention in public-service fields, but the size of any workforce effect is not quantified here. The title says Trump ended the program; the event details describe eligibility interpretations and an application freeze, which are not the same as repealing PSLF.
